base_method_text.title: Diffusion Model-Augmented Behavioral Cloning
base_method_text.summary:
Imitation learning addresses the challenge of learning by observing an
expert's demonstrations without access to reward signals from environments.
Most existing imitation learning methods that do not require interacting with
environments either model the expert distribution as the conditional
probability p(a|s) (e.g., behavioral cloning, BC) or the joint probability p(s,
a). Despite the simplicity of modeling the conditional probability with BC, it
usually struggles with generalization. While modeling the joint probability can
improve generalization performance, the inference procedure is often
time-consuming, and the model can suffer from manifold overfitting. This work
proposes an imitation learning framework that benefits from modeling both the
conditional and joint probability of the expert distribution. Our proposed
Diffusion Model-Augmented Behavioral Cloning (DBC) employs a diffusion model
trained to model expert behaviors and learns a policy to optimize both the BC
loss (conditional) and our proposed diffusion model loss (joint). DBC
outperforms baselines in various continuous control tasks in navigation, robot
arm manipulation, dexterous manipulation, and locomotion. We design additional
experiments to verify the limitations of modeling either the conditional
probability or the joint probability of the expert distribution, as well as
compare different generative models. Ablation studies justify the effectiveness
of our design choices.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces Diffusion Model-Augmented Behavioral Cloning (DBC), a novel imitation learning framework that combines the efficiency of modeling the conditional probability p(a|s) with the generalization ability of modeling the joint probability p(s, a) of expert demonstrations. DBC uses a diffusion model to capture expert behaviors and trains a policy to optimize both the behavioral cloning loss and a proposed diffusion model loss.
base_method_text.methodology: DBC employs a diffusion model trained on expert demonstrations to estimate the likelihood of state-action pairs. It then trains a policy to optimize both the behavioral cloning (BC) loss, which models the conditional probability p(a|s), and a diffusion model loss, which leverages the joint probability p(s, a) to guide policy learning. The diffusion model is based on Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs).
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The framework was evaluated on continuous control tasks, including navigation (MAZE), robot arm manipulation (FETCH PICK), dexterous manipulation (HAND ROTATE), and locomotion (CHEETAH, WALKER, ANTREACH). Baselines included Behavioral Cloning (BC), Implicit BC (IBC), and Diffusion Policy. Performance was measured using success rate and return. Ablation studies were conducted to justify design choices and investigate hyperparameter effects.
base_method_text.limitations: The proposed framework is designed to learn from expert trajectories without interacting with environments, so it cannot learn from agent trajectories. The framework inherits biases exhibited by the expert demonstrators, which can manifest as sub-optimal, unsafe, or even discriminatory behaviors.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research could extend the method to incorporate agent data for potential improvement when interacting with environments is possible. Addressing the biases inherited from expert demonstrators is also crucial, potentially through ongoing research in mitigating bias and promoting fairness in machine learning.

add_method_texts.title:
The Stronger the Diffusion Model, the Easier the Backdoor: Data
  Poisoning to Induce Copyright Breaches Without Adjusting Finetuning Pipeline
add_method_texts.summary:
The commercialization of text-to-image diffusion models (DMs) brings forth
potential copyright concerns. Despite numerous attempts to protect DMs from
copyright issues, the vulnerabilities of these solutions are underexplored. In
this study, we formalized the Copyright Infringement Attack on generative AI
models and proposed a backdoor attack method, SilentBadDiffusion, to induce
copyright infringement without requiring access to or control over training
processes. Our method strategically embeds connections between pieces of
copyrighted information and text references in poisoning data while carefully
dispersing that information, making the poisoning data inconspicuous when
integrated into a clean dataset. Our experiments show the stealth and efficacy
of the poisoning data. When given specific text prompts, DMs trained with a
poisoning ratio of 0.20% can produce copyrighted images. Additionally, the
results reveal that the more sophisticated the DMs are, the easier the success
of the attack becomes. These findings underline potential pitfalls in the
prevailing copyright protection strategies and underscore the necessity for
increased scrutiny to prevent the misuse of DMs.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces SilentBadDiffusion, a novel backdoor attack method targeting text-to-image diffusion models. This method aims to induce copyright infringement by strategically embedding connections between copyrighted information and text references in poisoning data, without requiring access to the training or fine-tuning processes. The research demonstrates the vulnerability of diffusion models to generating copyrighted images when triggered by specific prompts, highlighting potential pitfalls in copyright protection strategies.
add_method_texts.methodology: The SilentBadDiffusion method involves three stages: (1) Poisoning Data Generation, which includes Element Decomposition using a Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM) and semantic segmentation to identify and segment visual elements, and Poisoning Image Generation using a Large Language Model (LLM) and an inpainting model to create cohesive image-text pairs; (2) Model Training using the poisoned dataset; and (3) Inference Stage, where specific prompts trigger the compromised model to generate copyright infringing images. The method exploits the diffusion models’ understanding of textual references and visual elements to compose copyrighted images.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The experiments were conducted on Stable Diffusion models (v1.1 to v1.5) using the Pokemon BLIP Captions dataset and a subset of the LAION Aesthetics v2 6.5+ dataset, as well as the COYO-700m dataset. The attack success was evaluated using the Self Supervised Copy Detection (SSCD) metric, with a threshold of 0.5 indicating copyright infringement. The Copyright Infringement Rate (CIR) and First-Attack Epoch (FAE) were used to quantitatively assess the attack's effectiveness.
add_method_texts.limitations: The approach assumes that copyright images are decomposable into distinct elements. The study acknowledges ethical and legal concerns associated with datasets like LAION and Pokemon, which contained problematic content. The effectiveness of the attack is also dependent on the composition ability of the diffusion model and may not be as effective with less advanced models or when using a significantly reduced portion of poisoning data.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring a broader range of copyright targets, leveraging optimization techniques to integrate copyright information by updating pixel-wise values of the training data, and investigating style-attack and multiple-backdoors attack scenarios. Additionally, further investigation into the memorization mechanisms of diffusion models and their potential for few-shot generalization could provide valuable insights into developing protection mechanisms.

base_experimental_code:
Based on the repository content, there's no direct code implementation of a diffusion model. However, the 'gail.py' file implements Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL), which shares the goal of imitation learning with DBC. Key elements of GAIL implementation include:

1.  Discriminator Class:
    *   Defines a discriminator network to distinguish between expert and policy-generated state-action pairs.
    *   Includes methods for computing gradient penalties to improve training stability.
2.  Update Method:
    *   Updates the discriminator based on expert and policy data.
    *   Computes GAIL loss, combining binary cross-entropy losses for expert and policy data with a gradient penalty.
3.  Expert Dataset Class:
    *   Defines a dataset class to load expert trajectories from an h5 file.
    *   Includes sub-sampling and indexing logic for efficient data access.

While this code doesn't directly implement DBC, it provides a GAIL framework, an alternative approach to imitation learning that addresses similar challenges.
base_experimental_info:
The provided repository doesn't contain a direct implementation of the DBC method. However, the GAIL implementation includes elements that are relevant to imitation learning experiments. Specifically, the gail.py file contains:

1.  Expert Data Loading: The ExpertDataset class loads expert trajectories from an h5 file, which would be necessary for any imitation learning experiment.
2.  Rollout Data Generation: The policy_data_generator yields state-action pairs from the agent's rollouts.
3.  Discriminator Training: The update method trains a discriminator to distinguish between expert and policy-generated data, which is a key component of GAIL and related imitation learning methods.

The arguments.py file also defines several relevant hyperparameters, including:

*   --gail: Enables imitation learning with GAIL.
*   --gail-experts-dir: Specifies the directory containing expert demonstrations for GAIL.
*   --gail-batch-size: Sets the batch size for GAIL training.
*   --gail-epoch: Sets the number of GAIL epochs.
